opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a really central question, and it's something we've been thinking about a lot since the catastrophic overtraining work.

The basic phenomenon we observed is that as you pre-train on more and more tokens, the base model keeps getting better by standard metrics, but past a certain point the model becomes harder to fine-tune well. After fine-tuning, it can actually end up worse, both on the downstream task and in how much it retains of its general capabilities. Our framing for this is progressive sensitivity: the longer you pre-train, the more sensitive the parameters become to perturbation. Fine-tuning is a perturbation, so it does more damage to what the model learned in pre-training.

The relationship between the two distributions matters a lot. The intuition is that if the fine-tuning distribution is very close to the pre-training distribution, you don't need to move the parameters very far. You're making a small, well-aligned update, and the sensitivity doesn't hurt you as much. When the fine-tuning data is further from what the model saw in pre-training, you need larger updates. A specialized domain, a different format, or an instruction-following style that differs from web text are all examples. Those updates interact badly with the increased sensitivity, and that's when you see the degradation kick in earlier and more severely.

So one way to think about it is that the inflection point, the token budget past which more pre-training starts to hurt, isn't a fixed number. It depends on how far you're going to have to travel during fine-tuning. A bigger distribution shift effectively pulls that inflection point earlier.

There's also an interplay with the learning rate and regularization during fine-tuning. If you fine-tune with a small enough learning rate, you can delay some of the forgetting, but then you may not adapt enough to the new task. With a larger shift you're stuck in a tighter tradeoff between adapting and preserving. Mitigations like lower learning rates or regularizing toward the base model help, but they don't fully eliminate the effect.

The broader takeaway for me is that we shouldn't evaluate pre-training purely by base-model metrics. What we really care about is how adaptable the model is to the downstream distributions people will fine-tune on. That suggests designing pre-training with the eventual fine-tuning distribution in mind. Examples include mixing in data that's closer to downstream use, or using training procedures that keep the model in a less sensitive region of parameter space, rather than just scaling tokens and assuming more is always better.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes increased parameter sensitivity after longer pre-training from the larger updates required when the fine-tuning distribution is farther away.

r002.rationale: It says a small learning rate can delay forgetting but may limit adaptation; it does not identify good fine-tuning at a small learning rate as a proxy for requiring little model change.

r003.rationale: It explains that fine-tuning close to the pre-training distribution needs only a small, aligned update, reducing the harm from sensitivity.

r004.rationale: It states that a larger distribution shift moves the overtraining inflection point earlier and leads to worse fine-tuned performance.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss whether intuitive judgments of distributional closeness may differ from how information is represented internally by the model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of the more subtle parts of the story, and I think it's where a lot of the intuition from the "more pre-training is always better" worldview breaks down.

So the core phenomenon we called catastrophic overtraining is that as you keep pre-training a model on more and more tokens, it becomes progressively more sensitive to any kind of perturbation of its parameters. Fine-tuning is a perturbation. So even though the base model keeps getting better on pre-training loss, the model you get after fine-tuning can actually get worse past some point. We saw this with OLMo, for example, where the 3 trillion token checkpoint ended up worse after instruction tuning than the 2.3 trillion token checkpoint on a bunch of downstream tasks.

Now, where the distribution relationship comes in is in what fine-tuning is actually doing to the model. If the fine-tuning distribution is close to pre-training, the gradient updates you take are kind of aligned with what the model already knows. You're nudging it, you're not fighting it. The parameter movement needed to fit the fine-tuning data is small, and so the degradation you get from this heightened sensitivity is also small.

But when the fine-tuning distribution is far from pre-training, you need larger updates to actually fit the new task. And that's exactly the regime where the extended pre-training hurts you the most, because now you're taking a big step on a model that's become very brittle. What we see is that the forgetting of the pre-training capabilities is much more pronounced, and sometimes the fine-tuning task performance itself is worse too, because the model is in some sense less adaptable.

One way I like to think about it is that longer pre-training is kind of sharpening the model into a particular solution. It's getting more and more specialized to the pre-training distribution, and the loss landscape around that solution is getting more fragile. So if your downstream use is close to that distribution, great, you benefit from the sharpening. If it's not, you'd often actually prefer a less-trained base model that's sort of more malleable.

And I'd add one caveat, which is that this interacts with how you fine-tune. You can partially mitigate it with smaller learning rates or regularization toward the base weights, but that's a trade-off, because then you fit the downstream task less well. So I don't think the fix is purely on the fine-tuning side. I think it genuinely changes how we should think about what the right pre-training budget is, given what you're going to do with the model afterward.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes increased sensitivity to parameter perturbations from the size of the updates needed to fit fine-tuning data.

r002.rationale: It mentions smaller learning rates as a mitigation, but does not identify good performance at a small learning rate as a proxy for needing little model change.

r003.rationale: It says close distributions yield aligned updates and small parameter movement, reducing degradation from extended pre-training.

r004.rationale: It explains that distant distributions require larger updates and that extended pre-training can then worsen post-fine-tuning performance.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss whether intuitive judgments of distributional closeness match how the model internally stores information.

astra-6.text:
I think the relationship between those distributions is really central. Pre-training gives you a model that’s very good on one distribution, and then fine-tuning asks you to adapt it to another. So the question isn’t just whether more pre-training improves the base model; it’s whether those improvements survive the adaptation process.

With catastrophic overtraining, you can have a model that’s better before fine-tuning but worse afterward. One way to think about that is that additional pre-training has made the model more sensitive to the changes introduced during fine-tuning. If the fine-tuning distribution rewards behavior that conflicts with what you want to preserve from pre-training, that sensitivity can become a problem.

But I wouldn’t reduce it to a rule that more distribution shift necessarily means more catastrophic overtraining. It matters what’s shifting, which capabilities you evaluate, and how you fine-tune. The important thing is to study the whole pipeline: more pre-training can improve the starting point without improving the model you ultimately deploy.

r001.rationale: The response mentions sensitivity to changes during fine-tuning, but does not distinguish tolerance for parameter changes from how much change adaptation requires.

r002.rationale: It does not identify strong fine-tuning performance at a small learning rate as a proxy for requiring little model change.

r003.rationale: It does not explain that nearby pre-training and fine-tuning distributions can avoid catastrophic overtraining because they require little model change.

r004.rationale: It says more pre-training can yield a worse model after fine-tuning, but does not connect that outcome to larger distribution shifts or state that additional tokens can eventually worsen fine-tuned performance.

r005.rationale: It does not address whether intuitive judgments of distributional closeness reflect how the model internally stores information.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that more pre-training doesn’t necessarily make the model equally easy to adapt to every downstream distribution. You’re improving it on the pre-training distribution, but fine-tuning is asking it to do something potentially different. So the relationship between those distributions matters a lot.

If they’re closely aligned, you’d generally expect improvements from pre-training to transfer more directly. But if fine-tuning requires changing behaviors that pre-training has strongly reinforced, additional pre-training could make that adaptation harder. You could then have a model that looks better before fine-tuning but performs worse afterward—that’s the kind of reversal we’re concerned about with catastrophic overtraining.

I wouldn’t reduce that relationship to a single measure of distribution shift, though. What matters is which features and behaviors transfer, which ones need to change, and whether the fine-tuning data and procedure can make those changes. So I’d think of it as an interaction between the pre-training distribution, the downstream task, and how you adapt the model.

r001.rationale: It discusses how pre-training can make adaptation harder, but does not distinguish tolerance to parameter changes from the amount of change needed to adapt.

r002.rationale: It does not mention small learning rates or use fine-tuning performance at a small learning rate as a proxy for how much change is required.

r003.rationale: It says close alignment can help improvements transfer, but does not explain that little model change is required or that this avoids catastrophic overtraining.

r004.rationale: It contrasts aligned distributions with fine-tuning that requires changing strongly reinforced behaviors, and says additional pre-training could make adaptation harder and lead to worse post-fine-tuning performance.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss whether intuitive judgments of distributional closeness match how the model internally stores information.
